title: The Misguided Democratic Opposition to Permitting Reform
text:
In a break with Congress’s Orwellian naming conventions, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is genuinely bipartisan, pro-affordability, and would create some jobs. Although affordability is a popular concept—the entire Democratic Party campaigned on it in the midterm elections—it isn’t easy to execute. Bringing down inflation by reducing the budget deficit would require painful choices to raise taxes or cut spending. Ending the Iran war or President Trump’s tariffs would be somewhat easier policy choices, but even those moves, while the right thing to do, have trade-offs: Submitting to Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz would enrich Iran and impose tolls on energy; eliminating the tariffs would upset some labor unions.

 There is probably just one simple method to make life more affordable for Americans without sacrifice: support permitting reform. Incredibly, Democrats in Congress cannot decide whether to help pass it.

 The permitting bill, which recently passed the Senate, is designed to streamline the process for building large-scale infrastructure, especially energy projects. The Democrats supplied 31 of the 33 “no” votes the bill received in the Senate. The split caucus is one reason House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has not yet indicated what posture he plans to take on the bill, and it is possible that, without his active support, it will die.

 Two of its co-sponsors, Senators Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, are among the Democratic Party’s most devoted environmentalists. Their desire to pare back regulation may sound startling. But, like many green-energy champions, they have come to recognize that decarbonizing the economy requires rapidly building a new electrified infrastructure with solar power, wind power, charging stations, and transmission lines to connect it all. Current regulations make that basically impossible.

 [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] 

 A series of laws dating back to the 1970s erected elaborate legal hurdles to building new housing and infrastructure. The real cost of highways tripled within a generation after the ’60s, and the United States has built one new airport during this time. The worst culprit is the National Environmental Policy Act of 1970, which originally required short environmental-impact statements for any project on public land, but has since swelled into a lawsuit machine that demands thousands of pages of statements and years or decades of hassle. California has spent billions of dollars over two decades on a goal of building high-speed rail with virtually nothing to show for the time and money and little prospect of eventual completion. Heinrich’s interest in reform grew out of a 17-year ordeal to build a wind farm and transmission lines.

 Despite having the word environmental in its title, the NEPA is not really an environmental law. It is a law that imposes forbidding regulatory processes on any project involving federal land. “Environmental” review held up congestion pricing—a climate-friendly traffic-reduction policy—in New York City for years. Paradoxically, environmental review can be used to block even purely conservationist projects such as restoring wetlands or protecting the Great Lakes from an oil pipeline. Anything that changes federal land use can be targeted with expensive litigation by anybody who wants to block it.

 The Biden administration authorized several hundred billion dollars in green-energy investments, only to recognize that little of the spending would materialize unless permitting could be drastically sped up. That realization inspired several efforts to pass permitting reform, of which the BAAJA is the latest and most promising. According to credible estimates , the permitting reforms in BAAJA would reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and bring down the cost of energy without spending any taxpayer dollars.

 This makes permitting reform an incredibly rare opportunity to press the “lower costs” button. The bill has the support of clean-energy manufacturers, the AFL-CIO—whose members would benefit from the construction boom it would allow—and some environmental groups.

 The primary source of opposition is the movement that built the 1970s legal architecture—groups such as the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council, which continue to exert influence over the Democratic Party. These organizations have decided that the permitting process, with its opportunities for interminable litigation, represent democracy in its purest form.

 Most of the groups themselves were founded in an era when preserving the built environment as it existed at the time, rather than climate change (which was a marginal concern before the 21st century), was the environmental movement’s preeminent objective. The NRDC was founded out of a movement to block a New York hydroelectric power station—that is, a source of low-carbon energy. These organizations use laws such as the NEPA to file lawsuits to block development, especially (but not exclusively) fossil-fuel infrastructure.

 Because the BAAJA would apply to all energy technologies, it would allow more fossil-fuel energy as well as more green energy. The net effect would likely be to reduce emissions by favoring wind and solar, which desperately need new transmission lines to move power from states that have lots of wind and sun to states that don’t. Solar energy, in particular, is getting dramatically cheaper, which means it is likely to replace fossil-fuel sources as long as new infrastructure is possible to build.

 Because fighting climate change, promoting affordability, and allowing the government to build things again are all popular causes, the movement against the bill has treaded carefully in its public messaging. Opponents have frequently insisted that their goal is not to block permitting reform, but to stop this version so that Congress can write a better and more progressive bill.

 This is a familiar ploy. In the past, conservative opponents of health-care reform have used the same message to run out the clock. When a hard-fought compromise measure emerges from Congress, its opponents will piously insist that Congress should simply start over. In reality, Trump is not going to sign a left-wing permitting bill that singles out fossil fuels for punishment.

 In October, during a private conference call of green groups opposing the bill, an organizer confessed, “This is an effort to stop this bill, not to make it better.” The details of the call were leaked to Joshua Siegel of Punchbowl News , probably by a mortified participant. Some of the groups that participated in the call continue to publicly insist they want to block the bill only so that Congress could improve it, even after their scheme was exposed.

 Senator Jeff Merkley of Oregon, who has sought to prolong the process as Congress’s legislative calendar runs out, told Siegel that his goal is merely a “democratic process where stakeholders can come and share their thoughts.” Ironically, the tactic of preserving the status quo through delay in the guise of democratic participation is precisely how the NEPA works.

 [ Listen: Did Democrats win—or did Trump lose? ] 

 The anti-BAAJA groups have connected their cause to a broader strain of anti-corporate populism and to generalized anger with capitalism. They have argued that the bill would enable more data-center construction, even though data centers are generally built on private land and thus unaffected by NEPA. (This is why so many of them have sprung up quickly.) Newly elected Representative William Lawrence , a former member of the Democratic Socialists of America and a founder of the left-wing Sunrise Movement, depicted the problem as economic development of any kind. “My constituents have seen grand promises made and broken before. They have seen, for 50 years, the profits from development go to the wealthiest, usually investors from out of town, while the working and middle class have stagnated and declined,” he wrote on X. “I encourage you to see it as a vote of NO CONFIDENCE in the economy under current management.”

 Lacking confidence in the current economy is a sensible posture, but a bizarre argument for maintaining the status quo. Yet this is the position large chunks of the party’s left has talked itself into. The paradox is that federal regulations labeled as “environmental” are a barrier against environmental progress—and, by freezing the built environment in place, these regulations block all sorts of necessary change.

 Franklin D. Roosevelt helped end the Great Depression by hiring millions of people to construct public works. In 2009, the Obama administration hoped to replicate this feat, but quickly gave up when it realized that any new federal construction would require years of permitting before work could begin. (“There’s no such thing as shovel-ready projects,” President Obama lamented.)

 The technology for building roads, bridges, and dams had not regressed since the 1930s, but the legal environment had. The same barriers were in place a dozen years later when the Biden administration poured billions of dollars into a crash program to speed the green-energy revolution, and President Biden’s hope that he could show concrete results of his program—rural broadband, EV-charging stations, new ribbon cuttings of highways and bridges—evaporated. If those same barriers are in place the next time their party takes office, Democrats will have only themselves to blame.
